d.try: Open an atlas or a printed world map and count the countries on one continent, such as Africa or South America. Ask a friend to count the same continent without comparing. If your numbers differ, look closely at where you disagreed. Those spots are often the tricky cases that experts argue about too.
myth: Everyone agrees on exactly how many countries there are.
There is no single list. The UN has 193 members, but some places, such as Kosovo and Taiwan, run their own affairs and are recognised as countries by some governments and not others.

sec.t:
The number of countries has changed a lot. When the UN began in 1945, it had 51 members, including India, which joined before it was even independent. As [[@decolonisation|colonies in Africa and Asia]] won freedom in the 1950s and 1960s, membership grew fast.

In 1991 the Soviet Union broke up into 15 separate countries, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The newest UN member is South Sudan, which split from Sudan in 2011 after its people voted for independence.

Some places look like countries but belong to another. [[@world-greenland|Greenland]], the world's largest island, runs most of its own affairs but is part of the Kingdom of Denmark. [[@puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] and Guam are [[territory|territories]] of the USA. Hong Kong has its own money and sports teams but is part of China.

Then there are the four nations of the United Kingdom: England, [[@scotland|Scotland]], Wales and Northern Ireland. People there often call them countries, and they have their own football teams. But together they make up one member of the UN. Whether you call a place a country can depend on whether you are talking about law, sport or everyday life.

Countries come in wildly different sizes. [[@russia|Russia]] is the largest, about 1.7 crore km², so wide that it spans 11 [[@time-zones|time zones]]. India is the seventh largest.

At the other end, Vatican City is about 0.44 km², roughly the size of a large park. Monaco, on the French coast, is about 2 km². All its people could fit inside one big cricket stadium.

China and Russia each touch 14 other countries, more than anyone else. Some countries are completely surrounded by just one other: Lesotho sits entirely inside [[@south-africa|South Africa]], and San Marino and Vatican City inside Italy.

Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are "doubly landlocked". To reach the sea from either one, you must cross at least two other countries.

Sports bodies count differently again. FIFA, which runs world football, has more than 200 members, because England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each play separately. The Olympics welcomes teams from more than 200 places too. For a sports fan, the world has more countries than the UN says.

text: Fairy tales are old because they are easy to remember and fun to retell. They have simple shapes: three brothers, three wishes, a forest, a wicked giant, a clever youngest child. Anyone can carry one in their head and pass it on, without a book.

Many of the tales we know were written down only in the last 300 years. But that is just when collectors caught them. The stories themselves had been told aloud, by grandparents and travelling storytellers, for much longer. Some may be thousands of years old.

st.prompt: Where does the oldest known Cinderella-type story come from?

options.t: An ancient tale about a girl in Egypt, told by Greek writers
France in 1697
Germany in 1812

st.reveal: Greek writers about 2,000 years ago told of Rhodopis, whose sandal was snatched by an eagle and dropped in front of the king of Egypt. He searched for its owner and married her. A Chinese version, about a girl called Ye Xian, was written down in the 800s.

src: Graça da Silva S. and Tehrani J. (2016) Comparative phylogenetic analyses uncover the ancient roots of Indo-European folktales. Royal Society Open Science.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, fairy tale.
n.certNote: A 2016 study used methods borrowed from biology to suggest that some tales are thousands of years old. Other folklorists think the method can't be trusted that far back, because stories are easily borrowed between neighbours.

d.try: Ask the oldest person in your family to tell you a story they heard as a child. Write it down, then compare it with a fairy tale you know. Look for the same shapes, such as three tries, a magic helper or a cruel stepmother.
myth: The Brothers Grimm made up their fairy tales.
The Grimms collected tales from storytellers and older books. They did edit them heavily, and later editions became gentler and more suitable for children.

sec.t:
In 1697 a French writer called Charles Perrault published tales including Cinderella, Puss in Boots and Little Red Riding Hood. In 1812 two brothers in [[@germany|Germany]], Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, published the first volume of their collection. It included Hansel and Gretel, Rapunzel and Snow White.

The Grimms were language scholars. They believed old tales held clues to the past of the German language and people. They gathered stories from friends, neighbours and older books, then rewrote them over many editions.

In Bengal, Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumder collected tales from village grandmothers and published them in 1907 as Thakurmar Jhuli, "Grandmother's Bag". It is still a favourite, with its demons, princes and talking birds. India has many such collections, and an even older tradition of [[@storytelling-india|telling stories aloud]].

Folklorists, people who study traditional stories, sort tales into "types". Cinderella is a type. So is the dragon-slayer, and the clever animal who tricks a stronger one. One famous catalogue lists more than 2,000 types found around the world.

In 2016, a folklorist, Sara Graça da Silva, and an anthropologist, Jamshid Tehrani, tried something new. They treated tales like living things that [[evolve|evolve]], and compared versions in many related [[@languages-world|languages]]. They looked for which tales were shared by languages that split apart long ago.

Their study suggested that Beauty and the Beast and Rumpelstiltskin may be around 4,000 years old. A tale called The Smith and the Devil, about a blacksmith who outwits an evil being, might go back 6,000 years. Other experts are cautious. Stories jump easily between neighbours, so a shared tale does not always mean a shared ancestor.

sec.h: Why the same stories turn up everywhere
sec.t:
There are two main explanations, and both are probably true. Some stories spread from place to place with traders, travellers and marriages. A tale heard in a market could cross a sea in one lifetime. The [[@arabian-nights|Arabian Nights]] and the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]] both travelled this way, through many languages.

Other stories may grow up separately because people everywhere share the same hopes and fears. Losing a parent, being bullied by bigger siblings, getting lost, or rising from poverty to riches are worries in every culture.

Early versions were often much darker than today's films. In some old Cinderella stories the stepsisters are punished cruelly. In Perrault's Little Red Riding Hood, nobody comes to the rescue. The Grimms softened many tales in later editions, because by then parents were buying the books for children.

Writers keep inventing new fairy tales too. Hans Christian Andersen in Denmark wrote [[@myths-mermaids|The Little Mermaid]] and The Ugly Duckling in the 1830s and 1840s. They felt so traditional that many readers assumed they were centuries old.

text: Munshi Premchand was one of the greatest writers of modern Hindi and Urdu. He lived from 1880 to 1936 and wrote about 300 short stories and more than a dozen novels. His real name was Dhanpat Rai Srivastava.

Before him, much popular fiction in north India was about magic, kings and adventures. Premchand wrote about ordinary people instead: farmers, widows, schoolchildren, clerks and moneylenders. He showed their hopes and troubles honestly, with humour and kindness. Many readers still call him "Upanyas Samrat", the emperor of novels.

st.reveal: His friends buy sweets and toys and tease him. But Hamid had noticed his grandmother Amina burning her fingers at the stove. When he gives her the tongs, she cries, partly at his sacrifice and partly at his love.

sec.h: A teacher who wrote at night
sec.t:
Premchand was born in Lamhi, a village near [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]. His father was a [[@post-office|post office]] clerk. His mother died when he was about seven, and his father when he was a teenager, leaving the family poor.

He became a schoolteacher and later a deputy inspector of schools, writing stories in his spare time. In 1921, when [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] called on Indians to stop working for the British government, Premchand gave up his secure job. He spent the rest of his life writing, editing magazines and running a [[@printing-press|printing press]] that often lost money. In 1930 he started a Hindi literary magazine called Hans, meaning "swan". It was revived decades later and is still published.

Many Indian children meet Premchand in school. In Idgah, Hamid is a poor orphan who lives with his grandmother. On Eid morning, his friends set off for the fair with more money than him. He chooses a gift for her instead of a treat for himself. The ending makes readers smile and swallow hard at the same time.

Bade Bhai Sahab is about two brothers. The elder studies all the time and keeps failing, while the younger plays all day and keeps passing. Do Bailon ki Katha follows two bullocks, Hira and Moti, who escape and find their way home. Panch Parmeshwar asks whether friends can judge each other fairly in a village council.

His last finished novel, Godaan (1936), follows Hori, a poor farmer who dreams of owning a cow. Debt, [[@caste-history|caste]] and greed press in on him from every side. Premchand did not pretend [[@villages-india|village life]] was simple or peaceful. He showed unfair customs and the people who suffered under them.

In 1936, the year he died, he gave the main speech at the first meeting of the Progressive Writers' Association in Lucknow. In his speech he argued that writers should care about the lives of ordinary people and the problems of their society.

His stories keep finding new audiences. [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] filmed Shatranj ke Khiladi, about two noblemen so busy playing [[@chess-india|chess]] that they ignore the end of their kingdom. The film came out in 1977, more than forty years after Premchand's death.

text: Lassi and chaas are both drinks made from [[@curd-yogurt|curd]], the soft, sour, set milk that Indian families often make at home. The difference is mostly in how thick they are and what goes in.

Lassi is thick and creamy. Curd is whisked with a little water, then sweetened with sugar or flavoured with salt. In [[@punjab|Punjab]], it is often served in a tall steel glass or a clay cup, sometimes with a slab of malai on top. Chaas is thin and salty. More water is added, plus roasted cumin, ginger, green chilli or coriander. It is the everyday drink after a heavy lunch across much of western and southern India.

st.prompt: What makes curd, lassi and chaas taste sour?

options.t: An acid made by bacteria eating the sugar in milk
Lemon juice added at the dairy
The milk starting to go bad

st.reveal: Friendly bacteria feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and turn it into lactic acid. The acid gives the sour taste and also makes milk proteins clump into soft curd.

In the other, whisk three spoons of curd with half a glass of water and a spoon of sugar. Taste both and decide which is chaas and which is lassi.
myth: Drinking cold lassi or curd will give you a cold.
Colds are caused by viruses, which spread from person to person. A cold drink cannot give you one, though some people find cold food uncomfortable when they already have a sore throat.

sec.t:
Curd is made by tiny living things. When a spoon of old curd goes into warm milk, it carries millions of [[bacteria|bacteria]], mostly a kind called *Lactobacillus*. Overnight, they eat the milk's natural sugar, called [[lactose|lactose]], and turn it into lactic [[acid|acid]].

The acid makes the milk [[protein|proteins]] clump together into a soft, wobbly solid. It also makes it harder for harmful germs to grow, which is one reason sour milk foods kept better before fridges. This kind of change, made by [[microbe|microbes]], is called [[@fermentation|fermentation]]. The same process gives us idli batter, cheese and bread.

The bacteria work best when they are warm, at about the temperature of your own body or a little above. That is why curd sets in a few hours in May but can take all night in a north Indian winter. Some families wrap the pot in a cloth or tuck it near the stove to help. If the milk is too hot, it kills the bacteria, and nothing sets at all.

{{story:microbes-friendly}}

In many Indian villages, butter is made by churning curd with a wooden churner called a madhani or ravai. Turning it back and forth for a long time knocks the fat droplets together until they form lumps of white butter. These are lifted out, and some are slowly heated to make ghee.

What is left in the pot is real buttermilk: thin, tangy and low in fat. That is the original chaas. Today, most people just thin curd with water instead. In the United States, "buttermilk" in a carton is usually milk soured with added bacteria, used in pancakes and fried chicken more than as a drink.

Chaas changes its name, and its flavour, from state to state. In Gujarat it is chaas, often with a pinch of black salt. In Tamil Nadu it is neer mor, spiced with [[@curry-leaves|curry leaves]], ginger and asafoetida. In Karnataka it is majjige, and in Maharashtra taak. In Punjab and Haryana it is chhachh, drunk in large brass glasses in summer.

Lassi changes too. [[@mango-tree|Mango]] lassi is popular in Indian restaurants from London to New York, and many Americans think of it as India's national drink. In Amritsar, lassi shops pour it so thick that a spoon can almost stand in it.

Today, big dairies pack chaas into pouches and bottles. [[@amul|Amul]], the farmers' [[cooperative|cooperative]] from Gujarat, sells a spiced buttermilk that sits in shop fridges across India. Many smaller dairies do the same.

The drinks are cooling in a hot [[climate|climate]] partly because they are mostly water with a little salt, which helps the body replace what it loses in sweat. Nutrition experts also point out that curd drinks contain protein, calcium and, if they have not been heated, living bacteria. Whether you drink it sweet or salty is a question families argue about happily.

text: Almost any seed, nut or oily fruit can be squeezed for oil, and people around the world used whatever grew near them. Coconut palms line the coast of [[@kerala|Kerala]], so Kerala cooks with coconut oil. Mustard grows in the winter fields of the north and east, so Bengal, Bihar, Punjab and Assam use mustard oil. Groundnuts thrive in Gujarat, and sesame in Tamil Nadu.

Over centuries, each region's food grew around the taste of its oil. A fish curry from Kolkata wouldn't taste right without [[@mustard|mustard]] oil's sting, and a Kerala avial would seem odd without a final spoonful of [[@coconut|coconut]] oil poured over the top. On top of that, oils behave differently in the pan, so cooks pick different ones for frying, for tempering spices and for salads.

st.prompt: Why did cooks in Kerala traditionally use coconut oil, while cooks in Bengal used mustard oil?

options.t: They used what grew best around them
A king made a law about it
Coconut oil was cheaper everywhere in India

st.reveal: Coconut palms grow along the warm, wet coast of Kerala, and mustard grows well in the cooler winters of northern and eastern India. For centuries people cooked with the oil their own land produced, and their food grew up around its taste.

d.try: With a grown-up, put a spoonful each of two or three oils from your kitchen into small steel bowls, and place them in the fridge for an hour. Which ones turn cloudy or solid? Oils with more saturated fat harden first. Then smell each one at room temperature and describe the difference.
myth: All oil is the same; only the brand and the price change.

Oils differ in the fats they contain, how hot they can get before smoking, and how they taste. Mustard oil is sharp, sesame is nutty, and refined sunflower oil has almost no flavour. That is why recipes often name a particular oil.

sec.t:
All cooking oils are fats, built from smaller pieces called fatty [[acid|acids]]. Some fatty acids are "saturated", with straight shapes that pack together tightly. Fats with lots of them, like coconut oil, [[@butter-ghee|ghee]] and butter, turn solid when it is cool. Coconut oil hardens below about 24 °C, which is why a bottle goes white and cloudy in a north Indian winter. Oils with mostly bendy, "unsaturated" fatty acids, like sunflower and groundnut oil, stay liquid even in the fridge.

Oils also differ in their smoke point, which matters to every cook who has filled a kitchen with smoke. This is the temperature at which they start to break down and smoke. Refined oils, which have been filtered and cleaned, can usually get hotter than unrefined ones, so they suit deep frying. Unrefined, cold-pressed oils keep more flavour and smell.

sec.h: A world of oils, and a lot of palm
sec.t:
Worldwide, the oil produced in the largest amount is palm oil, from the fruit of the oil palm tree. Indonesia and Malaysia grow most of it. It is cheap and solid enough to use in biscuits, [[@maggi-noodles|instant noodles]] and soap. But clearing rainforest for palm plantations has destroyed [[habitat|habitat]] for orangutans and many other animals, so some companies now promise to buy only from farms that don't cut new forest.

India eats far more oil than its farmers grow. In 2024–25, it bought about 60% of its cooking oil from abroad, more than 16 million tonnes, much of it palm oil. In the USA, the most-used oil is soybean oil. Canola oil is also popular there. Canadian scientists bred it in the 1970s from rapeseed, a cousin of mustard, and named it after Canada.

Bodies need some fat. It helps you absorb [[vitamin|vitamins]] A, D, E and K, and builds the walls of every cell. Problems come from eating a lot of it, especially saturated fat and a type called trans fat. Trans fat forms when oil is partly hardened in factories, and small amounts form when oil is reused again and again for frying.

Since 2022, India's food regulator has limited trans fat in oils and fats to 2%. Doctors often suggest using a mix of oils rather than just one, using less of all of them, and not reheating the same frying oil many times. Many Indian kitchens keep two or three bottles on the shelf anyway: a neutral one for frying, and one that tastes of home.
